problem: Navigation diffusion policies (e.g. NavDP) are pretrained by imitating a privileged global oracle planner for a single nominal robot, so they fail in hard local-observation cases (dead ends, long-obstacle detours) and across embodiments. Prior RL for diffusion (DPPO, DSRL, DPMD) is unstable or explores poorly, giving only marginal gains.
motivation: Onboard robots only see partial local observations, so mimicking globally optimal trajectories causes decision ambiguity and suppresses recovery behaviors. RL post-training can adapt the policy to local observations and robot dynamics, but policy gradients through the diffusion chain are unstable and noise-based exploration breaks trajectory smoothness. Reweighted score matching is stable but its minibatch-normalized Q weights are uninformative for hard states.
key_idea: Post-train a pretrained navigation diffusion policy with reweighted score matching using within-state group-normalized Q-scores, while exploring through self-bootstrapped perturbation that mixes goal-conditioned and goal-agnostic samples from the same policy.
insight: Exploration quality is the main bottleneck: removing both the no-goal perturbation and the reverse flip collapses training (SR 6.23), and either one alone recovers most of the performance. Normalizing Q within each same-state candidate group beats DPMD's minibatch normalization (80.48 vs 71.57 SR in the 24-scene ablation), because hard states with uniformly low returns still give a useful relative signal. Policy-gradient (DPPO, 33.98 SR) and initial-noise-only (DSRL, 13.65 SR) methods are worse than plain SFT.
method: Self-bootstrapped perturbation: samples goal-conditioned and goal-agnostic trajectories from the same pretrained policy and mixes them as s⊙(τ_pointgoal + λ τ_nogoal), with a signed λ and Bernoulli(ε) sign flips of the x/y coordinates. This yields lateral, backward and detour candidates while keeping the trajectories smooth and feasible.

GQRM actor loss: samples N=64 candidates per state, scores them with the min of twin critics, and normalizes within the group (centered, scaled by c, clipped to [-h,h]). It keeps the top-5 candidates with positive advantage, then regresses the score/noise with weights exp(Q̃_G/λ). Only the 6 lowest-noise of 10 denoising steps are fine-tuned.

Embodiment-conditioned modulation: a learned robot embedding shifts the action tokens before the decoder and generates FiLM scale/shift on the decoder output, so a single shared NavDP-based predictor serves all embodiments.

Distributed RL framework in IsaacLab: 448 parallel environments over 56 scenes and rotating Dingo/Go2/G1 embodiments, with a shared DDP-synchronized actor/critics. Hierarchy is diffusion waypoint chunk → MPC (25 Hz) → embodiment-specific locomotion policy, and each 3 s chunk is one macro-step transition.
Reward: path progress computed from A* on an occupancy map (rewarded only for forward motion), plus goal arrival, collision, immobility, living and humanoid-fall penalties.
Closed-loop temporal guidance (RTC-style): at deployment, adds a gradient term during DDPM sampling that pulls the prediction toward the previously committed trajectory with decaying prefix weights.

setting.backbone: NavDP diffusion transformer policy (RL post-trained) with FiLM embodiment modulation; twin critics
setting.training_data: Pretrained NavDP (simulation-only imitation data), then about 12 hours of online RL in IsaacLab on 56 GRScenes-100 scenes (47 home, 9 commercial) with Dingo, Go2 and G1 embodiments
setting.action_space: waypoint chunks (H future waypoints) tracked by MPC into base velocities, executed by an embodiment-specific locomotion policy
setting.privileged: none at test time (A* progress reward and occupancy map only during RL training)

numbers.backbone: NavDP + GQRM RL post-training, FiLM, RTC guidance
numbers.extra: RL post-trained on 56 scenes for ~12 h; asynchronous evaluation

numbers.bench: other:IsaacLab GRScenes-100 point-goal navigation (24-scene training ablation)
numbers.eval_set_note: same held-out scenes; policy RL-trained on only 24-scene subset
10 trials per setting (lab/hall/office) on Turtlebot, Go2, G1; sim-to-real without fine-tuning

numbers_note: Custom IsaacLab/GRScenes-100 benchmark, not a canonical benchmark. Real-world per-cell success rates are given in Table 2; the abstract's 10%→65% for hard cases is not itemised in the tables.
results: In simulation X-NavDP improves NavDP from 61.20/58.95 to 84.28/77.19 SR/SPL, with the largest gains on humanoids (about 84% vs 64%/51%), and beats NavOL, SIDP and NavDP-RL on the settings they report. Real-world, it reaches 50-80% on hard lab/office layouts where NavDP, iPlanner and ViPlanner get 0%.
limitations: Uses only short-term temporal context, so long-horizon memory failures occur (e.g. returning along the original path when detouring around a wall).
Validated on three embodiments with predefined locomotion controllers; a new morphology needs its own pretrained low-level controller.
Struggles with transparent/hollow obstacles and narrow passages for the humanoid; real-world evaluation is only 10 trials per setting.
